notes.text: The following record includes the names of Noah’s sons and grandsons and their descendants (including some of the people groups who came from them). Here, **sons** means “descendants. The author is identifying these people as descendants of their ancestor Noah and his sons. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. or [and the sons they had]

notes.topic: These are the names of Javan’s sons
notes.text: These are the names of Javan’s sons, but the next two names are the names of people groups that descended from him. Alternate translation, with no comma following: [named Elishah and Tarshish, and he was the ancestor of]

Most translation teams transliterate people-group names in the Bible, but handle the suffix endings in different ways. For example, you could: (1) transliterate the Hebrew plural suffix “-im”; or (2) use a suffix that your language has for names of people groups (such as “-ites” in English); or (3) translate “-im” as “people” or “people group.” Try to be consistent in how you handle people group names throughout this chapter and the rest of the book of Genesis.
Your language may have its own terms or expressions for these relationships.

notes.topic: There were other mighty men before Nimrod
notes.text: There were other mighty men before Nimrod, but apparently he was the first one to have a kingdom (verse 10). or [a powerful king]

notes.topic: who was the first person to be
notes.text: The Hebrew text is ambiguous here. It could mean: (1) “who was the first person to be” or (2) “who became”
Shinar is another name for the land of Babylonia. You could put that information in a footnote.

Throughout verses 13–18, translate the names of people groups in a way that is clear and natural in your language. See what you did in verse 4. Also consider what is the best way in your language to list the names in these verses. Some languages use a conjunction (like **and**) between names, while other languages only use a conjunction before the last name in the list, with commas between the other names.

In verses 16–18, the people group names are singular collective nouns in Hebrew (in contrast to the people group names in verses 4, 13–14 that are plural nouns). Most English versions translate these names with a plural “-ites” suffix so that it is clear that these names refer to more than one person.
In the Hebrew text, **to Shem** comes first in this sentence after **And**, to emphasize Shem.

The name **Arpachshad** is spelled as “Arphaxad” in many translations. Also, see how you spelled **Lud** in verse 10:13 (who is a different person with the same name). Be consistent with how you spell each name throughout the Bible.
The same person who is called **Mash** here, is referred to as “Meshech” in 1 Chronicles 1:17. To prevent confusion, some translations use “Meshech” here too, or they put that name in a footnote.
You can put the meaning of Peleg’s name in the text or in a footnote so that it is clear why he was given his name. See what you did for a similar case (Noah’s name) in Genesis 5:29.

notes.topic: Sephar might refer to a city
notes.text: Sephar might refer to a city, a mountain, or a region (that was named after the city or mountain).

notes.text: Consider again how you translated **nations** in verses 10:5 and 10:20, 31–32. If it would be more natural in your language, you could change the order of the phrases.
